title: The Untold Battle Behind Abner and Joab’s Deadly Rivalry
paragraphs: The Untold Battle Behind Abner and Joab’s Deadly Rivalry
There are some wars in Scripture that were fought with swords.
And then there are wars fought with grief.

The most dangerous battles in the Bible were not always between nations. Sometimes they happened between wounded men carrying loyalty, pride, vengeance, insecurity, political ambition, buried pain, and unresolved rage.
This is one of those stories.
Most people remember the moment Joab killed Abner.
Few people understand why.
Fewer still realize how terrifyingly human this story truly is.
Because beneath the bloodshed was something almost every person alive understands:
betrayal, competition, family loyalty, political tension, humiliation, revenge, and the unbearable ache of losing someone you love.
The rivalry between Abner and Joab was not simply military conflict.
It was a collision between two kingdoms, two philosophies of loyalty, two wounded identities, and two men who believed they were defending righteousness while slowly being consumed by vengeance.
And hidden beneath the surface of their story is a terrifying warning for every believer carrying secret anger while still calling themselves faithful.
This story begins in the ashes after King Saul’s collapse.
Israel was fractured.
The throne was unstable.
David had already been anointed by God years earlier through the prophet Samuel, but the kingdom had not yet fully become his.
Saul’s dynasty still had supporters.
One of the strongest was Abner.
Abner was not just another soldier.
He was Saul’s cousin.
Commander of Saul’s army.
A powerful political force.
A kingmaker.
His name in Hebrew is אַבְנֵר (Avner), meaning “Father of Light.”
But sometimes men with names connected to light still walk through terrible darkness.
After Saul died, Abner established Saul’s surviving son Ish-bosheth as king over Israel while David ruled Judah from Hebron.
This created a divided kingdom.
Two thrones.
Two governments.
Two military powers.
And standing at the center of David’s military structure was Joab.
Joab’s Hebrew name יוֹאָב (Yo’av) means “Yahweh is Father.”
Joab was David’s nephew.
Fierce.
Brilliant.
Dangerous.
Loyal beyond reason.
But also impulsive, ruthless, emotionally violent, and terrifying when driven by personal vengeance.
Scripture never hides the flaws of its heroes.
That is one of the greatest evidences of biblical authenticity.
The Bible does not behave like propaganda.
It exposes the ugliness of even the men God used.
That honesty is uncomfortable.
And necessary.
The rivalry exploded publicly in 2 Samuel chapter 2.
The forces of Joab and Abner met near the pool of Gibeon.
What began as tension escalated into catastrophe.
The conflict became so intense that Scripture says:
“The battle that day was very fierce.”
But then something deeply personal happened.
Joab had a younger brother named Asahel.
Scripture describes Asahel as being “swift of foot as a wild gazelle.”
Young. Fast. Driven. Probably eager to prove himself.
During the battle, Asahel pursued Abner relentlessly.
Abner repeatedly warned him to stop chasing.
The language in the Hebrew text carries urgency.
Abner did not appear eager to kill him.
In fact, Abner asked:
“Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I face your brother Joab?”
There is something haunting about that sentence.
Abner already knew what would happen if Joab lost his brother.
He understood the kind of man Joab was.
But Asahel refused to turn away.
Finally Abner struck him with the butt end of his spear.
The text is graphic.
The spear came out through Asahel’s back.
He collapsed.
Dead.
And in that moment, vengeance was born.
This is where the story stops being ancient.
Because this is where human nature enters.
Grief changes people.
Especially when pain is mixed with humiliation.
Joab did not merely lose a brother.
He lost him publicly.
Violently.
During political instability.
During national division.
During military conflict.
And unresolved grief can become a religion if a person worships their pain long enough.
Years passed.
War continued between the house of Saul and the house of David.
But then something unexpected happened.
Abner broke with Ish-bosheth.
After being accused regarding Saul’s concubine Rizpah, Abner became furious and decided to transfer his allegiance to David.
This was politically explosive.
Abner essentially held the ability to unite the kingdom under David.
And David received him.
Peacefully.
This is where the story becomes emotionally complicated.
Because David acted like a king.
But Joab reacted like an offended brother.
Those are not always the same thing.
When Joab discovered David had welcomed Abner instead of executing him, he exploded with suspicion and rage.
To Joab, this was unforgivable.
A political enemy.
The man responsible for Asahel’s death.
A former commander of Saul’s army.
And now David was making peace with him?
Joab accused Abner of being a spy.
But underneath the accusation was likely something deeper.
Joab did not want reconciliation.
He wanted justice.
Or at least what he believed justice looked like.
Many believers still struggle with this.
We say we want healing.
But secretly we want revenge wearing the clothes of righteousness.
So Joab took matters into his own hands.
Without David’s approval.
Without lawful process.
Without restraint.
He secretly sent messengers after Abner and brought him back.
Then Scripture says Joab took Abner aside “into the midst of the gate to speak with him privately.”
And there he stabbed him in the stomach.
The text specifically says:
“for the blood of Asahel his brother.”
This was vengeance.
Personal.
Calculated.
Cold.
And devastating.
The Hebrew concept behind “bloodguilt” and avenging blood is deeply important here.
Ancient Israel operated with family honor systems and legal structures surrounding the “go’el ha-dam” (גֹּאֵל הַדָּם), meaning “avenger of blood.”
But Abner had killed Asahel during battle after repeated warnings.
This was not murder in the same category as Joab’s assassination.
Joab blurred justice with personal hatred.
And that distinction matters enormously.
Because anger has a terrifying ability to rewrite morality inside the human heart.
People begin calling revenge “conviction.”
Bitterness becomes “discernment.”
Hatred becomes “standing for truth.”
And eventually the soul can no longer distinguish righteousness from emotional addiction.
David’s response to Abner’s death is one of the most emotionally revealing moments in the Old Testament.
David publicly mourned.
Wept.
Fasted.
And declared:
“Do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen this day in Israel?”
That sentence shattered the political narrative.
David refused to celebrate the death of a former enemy.
Why?
Because godly leadership does not feed on revenge.
David understood something many believers still struggle to learn:
You can defeat someone without hating them.
You can oppose evil without surrendering your soul to bitterness.
You can seek justice without becoming consumed by vengeance.
Joab won the moment.
But he slowly lost pieces of himself.
That is the hidden tragedy of revenge.
People think vengeance heals pain.
But most of the time it only extends it.
The rivalry between Abner and Joab is not merely history.
It is a mirror.
Some people reading this are carrying years of unresolved wounds.
A betrayal.
A humiliation.
A church split.
Family rejection.
Abandonment.
False accusations.
Broken trust.
And outwardly you still worship.
Still serve.
Still post Bible verses.
Still say “God is good.”
But inwardly your spirit has been feeding on silent resentment.
That hidden war eventually changes people.
It changes how they pray.
How they love.
How they lead.
How they trust.
How they hear God.
And sometimes the deepest danger is not open rebellion.
Sometimes it is unresolved bitterness hidden beneath religious loyalty.
The New Testament later addresses this same spiritual danger.
In Ephesians 4:26–27 Paul writes:
Then in Greek:
“μηδὲ δίδοτε τόπον τῷ διαβόλῳ”
“Mēde didote topon tō diabolō.”
“Do not give place to the devil.”
The word τόπον (topon) literally means territory, room, opportunity, foothold.
Unresolved anger becomes spiritual territory.
And that is exactly what happened with Joab.
He gave rage a permanent room inside his heart.
Even years later he still could not let go.
And eventually vengeance became part of his identity.
This is why Scripture repeatedly warns believers about bitterness.
Hebrews 12:15 says:
“See to it that no root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled.”
Notice the language.
Root.
Roots grow underground before they become visible.
Bitterness hides.
It spreads quietly.
And eventually it poisons entire relationships, churches, ministries, families, and generations.
Joab remained powerful for years.
But his life became marked repeatedly by bloodshed.
Eventually even David, near death, instructed Solomon regarding Joab’s violence.
The consequences of unresolved vengeance followed him to the very end.
Sin rarely stays contained.
Especially emotional sin.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Jesus entered a world filled with Joabs.
Men carrying rage.
Violence.
Ethnic hatred.
Political division.
Religious hypocrisy.
Personal revenge.
Yet on the cross, Jesus prayed:
“Father, forgive them.”
In Aramaic, one traditional rendering is:
“Abba, shboq lahon.”
Forgive them.
Not because the wounds were small.
Not because justice did not matter.
But because mercy would become greater than vengeance.
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Not pretending pain never happened.
Not calling evil good.
Not erasing justice.
But refusing to let hatred become lord over the human heart.
Many people know how to win arguments.
Few know how to surrender bitterness.
Many know how to expose enemies.
Few know how to pray for them.
Many know theology.
Few know forgiveness.
And perhaps that is why this ancient rivalry still feels terrifyingly modern.
Because every person eventually becomes either more like David…
or more like Joab.
One learns to surrender vengeance.
The other feeds it.
One grieves without becoming consumed.
The other allows pain to become identity.
One leaves justice in God’s hands.
The other takes the sword personally.
And hidden somewhere inside every wounded soul is the temptation to become Joab while still believing we are defending righteousness.
That is why this story matters.
Not merely as history.
But as warning.
As conviction.
As invitation.
Because some people reading this have been fighting invisible wars for years.
Wars nobody else sees.
Wars hidden behind smiles.
Behind ministry.
Behind success.
Behind “I’m okay.”
But tonight God may be exposing something buried deeply beneath the surface.
The wound you kept feeding.
The resentment you kept justifying.
The bitterness you kept baptizing with spiritual language.
And maybe this article found you because heaven is confronting the war inside your heart before it destroys what remains of your peace.
Be honest.
This hit harder than many expected.
Some wounds do not destroy people immediately.
They simply wait quietly until bitterness finishes the work.
